The CONTROL device formulation utilizes m-Br-PEACl at 2.0 mg/mL as a key additive in the perovskite precursor solution, alongside Cs₀.₀₅MA₀.₁FA₀.₈₅I₃ (1.65 mol/L), MACl (15.0 mg/mL), SAM 4,4,4-NA (0.5 mg/mL), and passivator PDADI (0.5 mg/mL). While m-Br-PEACl contributes to grain boundary passivation, its meta-bromine substitution introduces steric hindrance that limits optimal interaction with undercoordinated Pb²⁺ ions at perovskite surfaces and grain boundaries. This results in incomplete defect passivation, elevating non-radiative recombination losses. Consequently, the baseline device exhibits a VOC of 1.179 V and FF of 81.26%, indicating significant voltage and fill factor losses due to interfacial and bulk recombination. The meta-positioned bromine also impedes efficient charge transport across grain boundaries, contributing to series resistance that caps the FF. Although JSC remains high at 26.24 mA/cm², the unresolved defect density from suboptimal m-Br-PEACl passivation creates a trade-off where high current density cannot compensate for voltage and fill factor deficits, yielding a PCE of 25.147%.  

Replacing m-Br-PEACl with p-F-PEACl at 2.0 mg/mL addresses these limitations by leveraging para-fluorine substitution. The para-orientation enables planar molecular alignment with the perovskite lattice, enhancing binding affinity to Pb²⁺ defects through stronger electrostatic interactions without steric constraints. Fluorine’s higher electronegativity versus bromine promotes more effective passivation of ionic defects and suppresses halide vacancy migration, directly reducing trap-assisted recombination. This modification improves VOC by minimizing surface recombination losses and boosts FF by lowering series resistance through better hole extraction at grain boundaries. The para-substitution also optimizes film morphology by promoting uniform crystallization, further enhancing charge carrier mobility. A minor trade-off involves a slight reduction in JSC due to marginally increased optical absorption from the fluorine moiety, but this is outweighed by the gains in VOC and FF. The unchanged MACl concentration (15.0 mg/mL) maintains optimal crystal growth kinetics, while fixed SAM (4,4,4-NA at 0.5 mg/mL) and PDADI (0.5 mg/mL) concentrations ensure interfacial and bulk passivation synergies without introducing new variables.  

The optimized formulation delivers a VOC in the range of 1.166–1.200 V, reflecting suppressed non-radiative recombination, and a JSC of 25.39–25.79 mA/cm², accounting for the minor optical trade-off. The FF improves to 83.9–85.9% due to reduced series resistance and enhanced charge extraction. Collectively, these yield a PCE interval of 24.8–26.6%, with the upper bound confirming significant efficiency gains over the baseline. Implement the following composition adjustments: replace m-Br-PEACl with p-F-PEACl at 2.0 mg/mL in the perovskite precursor solution, maintaining all other concentrations (Cs₀.₀₅MA₀.₁FA₀.₈₅I₃ at 1.65 mol/L, MACl at 15.0 mg/mL, 4,4,4-NA SAM at 0.5 mg/mL, PDADI at 0.5 mg/mL) unchanged.
control_device_fabrication: The device shows the highest PCE of 25.147% with negligible hysteresis, a VOC of 1.17917 V, a JSC of 26.2444 mA/cm² and a FF of 81.2593%. The process involved first dissolving Cs0.05MA0.1FA0.85I3 at 1.65 mol/L to create the primary perovskite solution. Careful addition of 4,4,4-NA (0.5 mg/mL) as a SAM ensured improved interface quality. The addition of MACl (15.0 mg/mL) and m-Br-PEACl (2.0 mg/mL) were instrumental in fine-tuning the perovskite film's optical properties. A sequential spin-coating procedure was employed, first at 1000 rpm for 5 s, followed by 5500 rpm for 30 s. At the last 15 s of the second step, 150 µL CB was dropped as antisolvent. By subjecting the film to 110 °C for 15 min, the perovskite lattice attained its ideal orientation. The passivator PDADI (0.5 mg/mL) was introduced into the system to improve material properties. The passivation layer was spin-coated using 5000 rpm for 30 s. During spin-coating, 70 µL of passivator was introduced at 6 s. The final step involved annealing the passivation layer at 100 °C for 5 min. In details, SAM solution was spin-coated on the substrate at 3000 rpm for 30 s, and annealed at 100 °C for 10 min.
target_device_fabrication: The device shows the highest PCE of 25.7614% with negligible hysteresis, a VOC of 1.1862 V, a JSC of 25.5903 mA/cm² and a FF of 84.8668%. 1.65 mol/L Cs0.05MA0.1FA0.85I3 perovskite precursors were prepared. The addition of 4,4,4-NA (0.5 mg/mL) as a SAM was performed to optimize surface passivation and ensure improved interface quality. Then, around 15.0 mg/mL of MACl and 2.0 mg/mL of p-F-PEACl were also added into the mixed perovskite solution. The prepared precursor solution was spin-coated at 1000 rpm for 5 s and 5500 rpm for 30 s onto the substrate. At the last 15 s of the second step, 150 µL CB was dropped as antisolvent. The substrate was then transferred to a thermostatic heater and annealed at 110 °C for 15 min. For better device performance, a passivation layer of PDADI (0.5 mg/mL) was deposited through spin-coating. After cooled to room temperature, passivators were deposited by spin-coating with 5000 rpm. To enhance the passivation layer, 70 µL of passivator was dropped at 6 s during spin-coating. Passivator solution was spin-coated and annealed at 100 ℃ for 5 min. In details, SAM solution was spin-coated on the substrate at 3000 rpm for 30 s, and annealed at 100 °C for 10 min.
